title: Storm Adam floods, election pledges and invoicing delay
summary:
Storm Adam has left four people dead, with confinement orders across Valencia and Alicante provinces. We cover election promises, a proposed survivor pension expansion, the Verifactu delay, and practical updates on housing, banking and electric car subsidies.

Enjoying Spain Daily? Support us: https://buymeacoffee.com/spanified

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: People across Valencia and Alicante were told to stay indoors—

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: —as Storm Adam overwhelmed local rescue services.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Military teams had to join the rescue effort.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: We'll start with what happened, and the official guidance.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Good morning. It's Tuesday, the twentieth of October, and this is Spain Daily, from Spanified dot com!

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: I'm Dima, here with Inna. Today: survivor pension plans and another invoicing delay. First, Storm Adam.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Storm Adam has left four people dead, Europa Press reports. Yesterday, authorities ordered residents in a hundred and forty-five municipalities across Valencia and Alicante provinces to stay indoors. Military emergency teams joined rescues because local and regional services couldn't answer every call. Flooding also disrupted roads and power supplies in the Balearic Islands.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Oliva, in Alicante province, was one of the worst-hit towns, and people died there.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: People were being rescued from rooftops and vehicle roofs. Helicopters and boats were both involved.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Inna, what were authorities telling people in the affected municipalities to do?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: The instruction was to stay indoors. Check the official alerts for your area, including those from Aemet, Spain's weather agency.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: The government plans to bring a survivor pension decree-law to cabinet today, El País reports. It would cover unmarried couples with children after two years of proven cohabitation. For pension purposes, those couples would be treated like married couples and registered domestic partners. Parliament's standing committee would then need to validate the measure.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: For a surviving partner raising children, access to that pension can be a very immediate household concern.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: And proving the time living together would be central for families covered by this proposal.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: For businesses managing their paperwork, there's another change of timetable. Heraldo reports that Verifactu has been postponed again, from January next year to October twenty twenty-eight. The invoicing system would require businesses to send invoices immediately to the Tax Agency. Firms now have more time to buy equipment and software, but some already invested.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Oof. If you paid to get ready early, another delay must feel rather different from extra breathing room.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Exactly. And one quote even says the defrauder is being rewarded. hm

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Taxes are part of the election debate too. Europa Press reports that PP leader and prime ministerial candidate Alberto Núñez Feijóo signed a twelve-point pledge yesterday. Ahead of November twenty-ninth, he promises a million new homes, pension increases and lower taxes. His commitments also include changes to immigration policy and investment in water infrastructure.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: That's a broad pitch, Dima. Housing, retirement income and taxes all reach directly into household budgets.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: They do. But these are campaign promises, not measures in force. right The housing one is what people looking for a home will watch most.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Staying with campaign promises, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has pledged annual increases in the minimum wage if re-elected. According to 20 Minutos, he made the commitment at a rally in Valladolid yesterday. He promised four more years of pension increases too. Sánchez argued that higher workers' wages would help keep the public pension system solvent.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: So his argument connects today's pay packets with retirement income, rather than treating workers and pensioners as separate groups. mhm

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: That's his case. For someone earning the minimum wage, the annual commitment is the part closest to their monthly budget.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: The election could also change control of the Senate, Spain's upper parliamentary chamber. A Sigma Dos poll for El Mundo projects a majority for PP, Vox and UPN after November twenty-ninth. But the projected bloc remains at least six seats short of the hundred and sixty-one needed for Constitutional Court appointments.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Hold on. So what could PP and Vox still do before the vote?

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: They have a window, from the twenty-first to the twenty-sixth of October, to withdraw Vox candidacies in some provinces or run shared lists. interesting That way right-wing votes aren't wasted.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: There's a voting-rights case before the Constitutional Court as well. El País reports that a man granted Spanish nationality under the Ley de Nietos, the grandchildren law, wants to vote on November twenty-ninth. He seeks to join the ombudsman's appeal and overturn a Supreme Court suspension. The case is pending, and the suspension remains in place.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: That's a very concrete election question for someone who's gained citizenship: whether they can actually cast a ballot.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: It is. Voting day is the twenty-ninth of November, so the timing matters.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: In another court decision, Supreme Court judge Pablo Llarena has upheld the lifting of arrest warrants for former Catalan president Carles Puigdemont. Two former regional ministers are also covered, La Vanguardia reports. Llarena said Constitutional Court doctrine must apply despite his disagreement. The Supreme Court's trial chamber must decide on Puigdemont's amnesty. The order can still be appealed.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: What happens next with the amnesty decision itself?

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: That goes to the trial chamber, which legal sources expect to receive the finished case file next week.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: A housing dispute may also reach the courts. El País reports that Spain's employers' confederation plans to challenge the November eleventh general strike over housing. It argues the strike lacks a work-related motive. Unions registered it yesterday. The employers' board is due to debate the challenge tomorrow.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: For workers considering joining, the legal dispute adds uncertainty before the strike date.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: And a general strike could affect work and services across Spain, so the implications go beyond those taking part.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: The pressure behind the housing debate shows up in new figures from Oxfam Intermón, reported by El País. Housing costs push about seven hundred and seventy thousand workers into poverty. Once rent or mortgage payments are deducted from income, around three million workers are counted as working poor.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Having a job doesn't necessarily mean there's enough left after paying for a home.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: No. Looking at what's left after housing makes that pressure on working households much clearer.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: On access to care, the government says the dependency benefits waiting list has reached a record low. 20 Minutos reports around a hundred and thirty-five thousand people were waiting on September thirtieth. This count includes only people waiting longer than six months. Average processing times have also fallen.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: For electric car buyers, El País reports industry concern about a subsidy gap early next year. The Auto Plus purchase-aid programme runs until December thirty-first, with about seventy-one percent of its funds used. Car brands warn the election could delay support during the first half of next year.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: So after the programme ends in December, there's no new money yet?

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Not so far. That's why the sector is nervous about the election timing.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: And there's money on offer for switching bank accounts. Expansión reports payroll bonuses of up to seven hundred and fifty euros. Some commitments last as long as four years. Leaving early means repaying a proportional share, and many offers also require Bizum, the mobile payment service, bill payments or card use.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Ah, the bonus comes with a relationship. You need to like more than the welcome gift.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: You do. The account needs to suit your everyday banking, including those payment requirements and the commitment.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Today's immediate priority is the flooding, while election promises and changing deadlines shape the weeks ahead.
